title: Which block is colder?
hook: Metal feels cold and wood feels warm. So which block in the room is colder?

doesNotKnow: that objects left in one room reach the same temperature
that skin senses the rate heat leaves it (set by the material's conductivity and heat capacity), not the object's temperature

misconception: Metal in a room is colder than wood in the same room.
objective: The learner can explain that metal and wood in one room are at the same temperature, and that metal feels colder because it draws heat out of the skin faster.

claims.text: Objects left in the same room for a long time reach the same temperature, so a thermometer reads 20 °C on both blocks (stage: 'probe 20 °C' under each block; reveal: 'Your thermometer read 20 °C on both blocks').
claims.source: Thermal equilibrium (zeroth law of thermodynamics): any introductory thermodynamics text, e.g. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, chapter on temperature (fact-checker picks the edition). Brief: company/domains/briefs/physics.electricity.md round 3 #1. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Rests on derivation, not on Halliday et al. (no edition named; not opened, web blocked): a body with no internal heat source exchanging heat with a 20 °C room relaxes to 20 °C (heat equation with fixed-temperature surroundings, unique uniform steady state). Stage: deg(ROOM) prints 'probe 20 °C' under each probed block; reveal says '20 °C on both blocks' (probe-both is a required milestone). Support could be derivation.

claims.text: When two bodies touch, the contact temperature is Tc = (e1 T1 + e2 T2)/(e1 + e2) with effusivity e = sqrt(k rho c) (semi-infinite bodies, perfect contact).
claims.source: Carslaw and Jaeger, Conduction of Heat in Solids (2nd ed., 1959), two semi-infinite solids in contact; re-derived and simulated by finite differences in artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r3/check.mjs. Used in Demo.tsx `contact()`. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Re-derived: erf solutions for two semi-infinite bodies; flux continuity k1(T1-Tc)/sqrt(pi a1 t) = k2(Tc-T2)/sqrt(pi a2 t), and k/sqrt(a) = sqrt(k rho c) = e, so Tc = (e1T1 + e2T2)/(e1+e2), constant in t. Own explicit finite-difference run (skin/pine, 50 ms) gives 30.06 vs 30.29 analytic (interface discretisation). Carslaw and Jaeger not opened; verdict rests on the derivation. Demo.tsx contact() implements it.

claims.text: A 33 °C fingertip touching a 20 °C block settles at about 21 °C on aluminium (and on steel) and about 30 °C on pine (stage: 'skin 21 °C' / 'skin 30 °C'; reveal: 'its skin dropped to about 21 °C on the metal and only to about 30 °C on the wood').
claims.source: c2 with e = sqrt(k rho c): skin (k 0.37, rho 1,100, c 3,400) e = 1,176; aluminium (237, 2,700, 900) e = 23,998; plain carbon steel (60.5, 7,854, 434) e = 14,360; pine (0.12, 500, 1,600) e = 310. Tc = 20.61 °C (Al), 20.98 °C (steel), 30.29 °C (pine), shown with toFixed(0) as 21 / 21 / 30. Property values from Incropera et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, appendix A (steel row added by demo-builder; brief gave Al, pine, skin); skin and wood values vary and are illustrative. Node re-run by demo-builder 2026-10-14; brief's check.mjs gives the same 30.3 / 20.6. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node with the stated inputs: e skin 1,176, Al 23,998, steel 14,360, pine 310; Tc 20.61 / 20.98 / 30.29 -> '21' / '21' / '30' (toFixed(0)). Incropera not opened; I cross-checked the metal and pine inputs against an opened independent table instead: ht 1.2.0 (PyPI) insulation.py, ISO 10456 / ASHRAE rows: aluminium alloys (2800, 160, 880), steel (7800, 50, 450), southern yellow pine (500, 1630, 0.13), eastern white pine (400, 1630, 0.10). With those, Tc is 20.7 (Al), 21.1 (steel), 30.2-30.7 (pines) -> same 21 / 21 / 30. Skin values are unsourced (declared illustrative); the rounded results hold for skin e from 1,000 to 1,400 (Al 20.6-20.9, pine 29.8-30.6). Swap always re-touches the new metal, so label, skin line and arrow match.

claims.text: At the same moment, heat flows out of the finger about 4.6 times as fast into aluminium as into pine (4.4 times for steel); the arrow widths are drawn in that ratio (reveal: 'the metal's heat-flow arrow was 4.6 times thicker').
claims.source: Surface heat flux between two semi-infinite bodies at time t is q = (Ts - To) e_s e_o / ((e_s + e_o) sqrt(pi t)), so the ratio at equal t is [e_al/(e_s+e_al)] / [e_w/(e_s+e_w)] = 4.57 (steel 4.43), shown with toFixed(1). Demo.tsx `flux()`; arrow width = 3 px x ratio. Brief claim 4 (check.mjs: 4.6). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: [e_al/(e_s+e_al)]/[e_w/(e_s+e_w)] = 4.573 -> '4.6'; steel 4.433 -> '4.4'. Rect body width = 3 px x ratio (arrowhead adds a fixed 5 px each side, so only the shaft is in ratio). The reveal prints m.ratio for the metal currently recorded, so it says 4.4 if the learner swapped to steel. Note: the real-world ratio depends on the unsourced skin effusivity (3.9 at e_skin 1,000, 5.0 at 1,400 with the ISO 10456 metal and pine values); the learner sentence speaks of the drawn arrow, which is exact.

claims.text: Metal conducts heat away from your skin fast, so the skin cools; wood barely takes any, so the skin stays warm.
claims.source: Follows from c3 and c4: the metal's effusivity is about 75 times pine's, driven mainly by its thermal conductivity (237 vs 0.12 W/m K). Incropera et al., appendix A. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Follows from c3/c4: effusivity ratio Al/pine 77 (source field says 'about 75'; fine), driven by conductivity 237 vs 0.12 (ISO 10456 via ht: 160 vs 0.13). Nit, non-blocking: 'wood barely takes any' is strong; the stage shows wood drawing about 1/4.6 of the metal's flow and the skin falling 3 °C. Builder's call.

claims.text: Your finger senses heat leaving it, not the object's temperature.
claims.source: Skin thermoreceptors respond to skin temperature and its rate of change, so touch reports how fast the skin cools rather than the object's temperature: any physiology text on thermoreception (fact-checker picks the edition). The lesson does not name receptor types. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD. Physiology claim (thermoreceptors respond to skin temperature and its rate of change). The source field names no text ('fact-checker picks the edition'), and I could open none (web blocked: proxy 403 / DNS). Not derivable. To clear: a checker who can open a physiology text or review on thermoreception.

claims.text: Model stated on stage: 'Arrow: heat leaving the finger. Perfect contact, first seconds.' (semi-infinite blocks, no blood flow over the first seconds).
claims.source: Idealisations of c2 (brief claim 6). Over longer contact blood flow rewarms the skin and a finite block warms up; neither changes the comparison in the first seconds. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Stage chip after any touch reads exactly 'Arrow: heat leaving the finger. Perfect contact, first seconds.' (before: 'Same room, all day.'). contact() and flux() use the semi-infinite, perfect-contact, no-perfusion idealisation. Reveal needs touch milestones, so the chip is on stage when it opens.

recall.question: A tile floor and a wool rug have been in the same room overnight. Barefoot, the tile feels colder. Which one is at the lower temperature?
options: Neither: both are at room temperature
recall.why: Both have reached room temperature. The tile feels colder because it conducts heat out of your foot faster, and your skin senses heat leaving it.
